Agent-Driven Development with Workflow-Scoped MCP
Concept
A local MCP server exposes a small set of workflow verbs that an AI agent uses to move a feature through a defined state machine. A feature is the main entity: user-initiated, UAT-first, with automated merge to main and human security review downstream from merge.
The agent has broad latitude in the local zone (edit, commit, test) but can only touch shared systems through MCP verbs. Wrong actions are unrepresentable, not just rejected.
Feature Lifecycle
[no feature]
    │ start_feature
    ▼
[feature initialized: branch, state, infra, hosting]
    │ push_changes  ◄──┐
    ▼                   │
[deployed to test env]  │ (iterate)
    │                   │
    ├── abandon_changes ┘─────► [cleaned up, no merge]
    │
    │ accept_changes (UAT approved)
    ▼
[merge workflow: tests, fix loop, possible escalation]
    │
    ▼
[merged to main]
    │ (downstream, async)
    ▼
[human security review → release]
get_status is callable at any point and returns canonical state from git hash + Azure DevOps pipeline status.
Tool Surface
start_feature
Initialize a new feature workflow.

Inputs: human-readable feature name (from user)
Actions:

Sluggify name → branch name (e.g., "Add dark mode toggle" → feat/add-dark-mode-toggle)
Create context state record: {feature_name, branch_name, branch_slug, current_hash, created_at, status: "initialized"}
Create git branch off main
Provision branch-scoped resources: environment configs, secrets, any per-feature infrastructure
Initialize Firebase Hosting preview channel for this branch


Returns: feature context object (branch name, hosting URL placeholder, state handle)
Preconditions: no active feature in current workspace; user-provided name is non-empty and unique
Failure modes: name collision (suggest variant), resource provisioning failure (rollback partial state, return structured error)

push_changes
Accept new user input describing desired changes; agent plans and executes the work; deploy to test env.

Inputs: user's change description / instructions
Actions:

Agent plans the work: file edits, package additions, API integrations, etc.
Execute plan locally: edit files, run builds, run tests
Commit changes with a generated message tied to the user input
Push branch
Trigger deploy to Firebase Hosting preview channel
Update context state with new hash and deploy URL


Returns: deploy URL, summary of what changed, test results
Retry/escalation:

On build/test failure: agent attempts fixes, bounded retries
After N failures: notify prompt with structured failure context, OR call request_human_help if the failure pattern suggests blocker (missing API access, ambiguous requirement, etc.)


Preconditions: active feature exists; branch is in clean state for new commits

get_status
Read canonical state of the current feature.

Inputs: none (uses active feature context) or optional feature_id
Returns one of:

not_found — no feature with this context
initialized — branch and resources exist, no commits yet
building — push in progress, deploy pending
deployed — deployed to test env, ready for UAT review
failed — deploy or pipeline failed, includes failure details
merging — accept_changes in progress
merged — in main, awaiting downstream security review
released — security review passed, in prod
abandoned — cleaned up without merging


Source of truth: combines git state (hash existence, branch state) with Azure DevOps pipeline status; not a self-reported field
Side effects: none — pure read

abandon_changes
Clean up everything related to the current feature without merging.

Inputs: none (uses active feature context); optional reason for audit log
Actions:

Tear down Firebase Hosting preview channel
Remove branch-scoped environment configs and secrets
Delete remote branch (local branch retained for archaeology if user wants it)
Update context state to abandoned with reason
Log abandonment with reason


Preconditions: active feature exists; not currently mid-merge
Note: terminal state — feature cannot be resumed after this; user starts a new one if they change their mind

accept_changes
UAT-approved; merge to main with automated verification.

Inputs: none (uses active feature context); optional uat_approver identity if not inferred from session
Actions:

Clean up branch-related ephemeral infra (Firebase preview channel, branch secrets, test env configs) — same as abandon
Enter merge completion workflow:

Add/update tests covering the new changes if not present
Run full test suite + any required pipeline checks
On failure: agent attempts fixes (bounded retries) — this is the "fix PR loop"
If failure pattern persists past threshold: request_human_help with full context
If human help unavailable or rejects: abandon_changes as final fallback
On success: merge to main, update context state to merged




Returns: merge commit hash, summary of what shipped
Preconditions: feature is in deployed state, UAT approval recorded
Note: this is the irreversible action. The MCP refuses if preconditions aren't met — agent calling prematurely gets a structured "not ready, here's why" response

request_human_help
Explicit escalation. Not a failure — a valid workflow action.

Inputs: structured context (what was attempted, what failed, what's blocking)
Actions: notify the appropriate human channel; pause the workflow; surface context so a human can resume or redirect
Returns: acknowledgment + handle for tracking
When agent should call this: repeated failures of the same kind, ambiguous user input that can't be resolved by re-prompting, missing access/credentials, anything outside the paved path

State Tracked Per Feature
{
  feature_id: <uuid>,
  feature_name: <human readable>,
  branch_name: <full ref>,
  branch_slug: <sluggified>,
  current_hash: <git sha>,
  hosting_url: <firebase preview URL>,
  status: <see get_status enum>,
  created_at, updated_at,
  uat_approver: <identity if approved>,
  failure_count: <for retry bounding>,
  history: [list of state transitions with timestamps]
}
Stored locally per workspace; the MCP is the source of truth for state, not the agent's memory.
Design Properties Worth Naming

Feature is the unit, not commit/branch/PR. The verbs operate on features; git artifacts are implementation details the MCP manages
UAT comes from the user directly via accept_changes — there's no separate "request UAT" verb because the user is the UAT approver, and calling accept is their approval
get_status is the agent's source of truth. Agent should call it whenever uncertain rather than reasoning about state from local context
Cleanup is shared between abandon and accept because the ephemeral infra goes away in both cases — the only difference is whether merge happens
Retry bounds are MCP-enforced, not agent-judged. The agent doesn't decide when to give up; the MCP does, based on failure counts
Security review is downstream of merge and out of band — not in this tool surface. The merged main is what the security reviewer sees; that workflow lives elsewhere

Pros

Reviewer throughput up 3-5x via UAT-first filtering and narrowed security-only review scope
Right evaluator for the right question: user does UAT (behavior), security reviewer does safety, automation does correctness
Agent can't get lost: state machine + get_status mean there's always a defined "what's next"
Conventions enforced, not documented: team workflow lives in MCP verbs
Mechanism-agnostic: swap Firebase for another host, swap Azure DevOps for GitHub Actions — agent unaffected
Auditable by design: every consequential action is a structured call with logged arguments and state transitions
Cleanup is structural: abandoning a feature can't leak resources because cleanup is part of the verb, not a thing the agent has to remember
Escalation is a first-class action: request_human_help means "I'm stuck" is valid behavior, not failure

Cons / Tradeoffs

Code quality drift: no per-PR human quality review; acceptable for agent-maintained code, costly if humans dive in later
Test env must be production-faithful or UAT approvals don't predict prod behavior
Security reviewer is a downstream bottleneck — needs tooling support and discipline to avoid rubber-stamping
Post-merge security rejection is socially harder than pre-merge — needs clear contract that downstream review can still send things back (revert + re-do)
Loses traditional code review side benefits: mentorship, knowledge sharing, style consistency — irrelevant for agent code, costly in mixed teams
Workflow design taste required upfront: wrong verb set means agent can't complete legitimate work, or paved path has escape hatches that get used routinely
State management is real engineering: the MCP owns truth about feature state, must reconcile with git + pipeline reality, must handle interrupted workflows
No mid-workflow resume after abandon_changes: terminal state by design, but users will occasionally want to "undo abandon" — needs to be explicitly refused with the suggestion to start fresh
Retry bounding is a tuning problem: too aggressive and real fixable issues get escalated; too lenient and the agent thrashes

When This Pays Off
High-volume agent-generated changes, user is non-technical or focused on behavior rather than implementation, security review can be batched downstream, and "did we build the right thing" is genuinely uncertain at start. Overkill for solo experimentation or low-volume agent use.

# Coding Agent Assistance Platform

## Proposal

---

## Executive Summary

This proposal outlines an internal platform for assisting developers with AI coding agents in a way that produces consistent, pattern-adherent, auditable output. The core problem is not whether AI agents can write code — they can. The problem is that without organizational guardrails, agents drift from established architectural patterns, reinvent existing services, and produce work that requires substantial rework before it can be merged.

The proposed solution is a suite of **workflow-shaped MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers** fronted by **Apigee as an MCP gateway**, with identity managed by **Duende IdentityServer** federated to Google IAM. Behavior is guided by a checked-in `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` file in each repository and enforced by CI-level architecture tests. The platform is agent-vendor agnostic: any MCP-compliant client (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, others) can consume it.

The architecture has a single source of truth for identity (Duende), a single ingress for traffic (Apigee), and a defined human approval workflow for granting agents access to resources. There is no automatic privilege issuance anywhere in the system.

---

## Problem Statement

AI coding agents are now broadly capable, but their output quality in an enterprise codebase is shaped less by the model and more by the surrounding context, tools, and constraints. Three problems recur across teams adopting agents:

1. **Pattern drift.** Agents produce structurally valid code that violates established patterns — for example, writing logic into controllers instead of CQRS handlers, or creating new services where existing ones should be reused.
2. **Discovery failure.** Agents do not know which services, repositories, or handlers already exist in the codebase. They confidently create `UserNotificationService` next to an existing `NotificationService`.
3. **Governance and auditability.** When agents take actions in tools like Jira and Git, the audit trail typically attributes those actions to the developer who launched the agent, with no record of what the agent itself decided to do, or under what authorization.

Off-the-shelf coding agents do not solve these problems. They are model-and-harness products; the codebase-specific context is the consumer's responsibility to provide. This platform provides that context in a structured, enforceable, auditable way.

---
## Goals and Non-Goals

### Goals

- Reduce the rework cycle on agent-produced PRs by giving agents the same context a senior engineer would have on day one.
- Enforce architectural patterns (CQRS, service/repository structure, layer boundaries) such that drift is detected at CI time, not at review time.
- Surface existing services, handlers, and repositories to the agent so reuse becomes the path of least resistance.
- Provide an end-to-end audit trail tying every agent action to the human who initiated it and the authorization under which it was performed.
- Remain agent-vendor agnostic — any MCP-compliant client should be able to use the platform.

### Non-Goals

- Building a proprietary coding agent. The agent loop is commoditized; this platform consumes existing agents.
- Replacing developer judgment. The platform is a side-assistant in Phase 1, not an autonomous coder.
- Solving correctness through prompts alone. Prose guidance is necessary but insufficient; enforcement lives in code.
- Dynamic client registration. All agent identities are provisioned through a defined human approval process.

---

## Architectural Approach

The platform is layered. Each layer addresses a specific class of failure, and the layers compose.

### Layer 1: Behavior Guidance (`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`)

A checked-in markdown file at each repository root, following the AGENTS.md open standard. The file does three things:

- **References exemplar files.** Points to the canonical implementation of each pattern (a model CQRS command handler, a model service, a model repository). Also explicitly identifies legacy files the agent should not imitate.
- **References verification commands.** Specifies the exact lint, format, test, and architecture-test commands the agent must run to verify its own work. Instructions without verification commands are suggestions, not rules.
- **References scaffolding tools.** Directs the agent to use the platform's scaffolding MCPs for boilerplate generation rather than writing structural code by hand.

The file is owned, versioned, and reviewed like production code. A named owner per repository maintains it.

### Layer 2: Custom MCP Servers

The platform's primary deliverable. Each MCP is workflow-shaped, not API-shaped — tools are named after operations the team actually performs, not after raw API endpoints.

| MCP | Purpose | Backing |
|---|---|---|
| **Scaffolding MCP** | Generates structurally correct boilerplate for new CQRS commands, queries, services, and repositories. | Code generation. |
| **Discovery MCP** | Surfaces existing services, repositories, and command/query handlers. Returns usage signals (in-degree, last modified) so the agent can distinguish canonical from abandoned code. | Roslyn (.NET) symbol analysis. |
| **Pattern Retrieval MCP** | Retrieves exemplar code and documentation across repositories. Used for "how do we typically handle X" queries. | pgvector, semantic chunking, commit-hash-keyed index. |
| **Jira Workflow MCP** | Exposes specific workflow actions (e.g., `move_ticket_to_in_review`) rather than the full Jira API surface. Each action is a composite operation that updates status, assigns reviewers, links the PR, and posts notifications atomically. | Thin wrapper over Jira REST API. |
| **Git Guardrail MCP** | Exposes git operations with hard constraints: no push to protected branches, no force-push, all commits reference a ticket. Free-form git is not exposed. | Wrapper over git CLI. |

Each MCP is independently deployable, has its own audience identifier in Duende, and is reached only via Apigee. MCPs trust Apigee as the upstream auth terminator and focus on per-tool authorization and business logic; they do not duplicate JWT validation.

### Layer 3: Apigee as MCP Gateway

Apigee is the single ingress for all MCP traffic. It plays five distinct roles:

**Edge authentication.** Apigee validates every incoming token against Duende's JWKS using the VerifyJWT policy. Signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required scopes are checked at the edge. Tokens that fail validation never reach a backend MCP. JWKS caching, rotation, and validation are Apigee's responsibility; backend MCPs are not in the JWT business.

**Forwarded identity to backends.** Once a token is validated, Apigee forwards the request to the appropriate backend MCP over mTLS with a signed identity header containing the authenticated principal, the delegation chain, and the resolved scopes. The MCP trusts this header because it arrived over mTLS from Apigee and not from an arbitrary network caller.

**Pre-provisioned client credentials.** Agent credentials (`client_id`, `client_secret`, scope set) are issued in Duende through the human approval process described in Layer 4 below. After issuance, the credentials are stored in encrypted Apigee KVM, scoped per environment. The Apigee shared flow reads from KVM to acquire and refresh tokens against Duende. **There is no dynamic client registration.** An agent that doesn't have pre-provisioned credentials in KVM cannot operate, and Apigee has no path by which to create credentials on its own. Duende remains the single source of truth for client identity and entitlement.

**Model Armor as a shared flow.** A shared flow applies Model Armor inspection on inbound tool arguments and outbound tool results, configured per-MCP based on risk profile:

- High-risk MCPs (Jira returning external content, Git accepting commit messages): full inspection, fail closed.
- Low-risk MCPs (Discovery returning your own codebase, Scaffolding generating boilerplate): minimal or no inspection.
- Autonomous-mode traffic: fail closed by default. Interactive-mode traffic with a human watching may fail open with annotation, by explicit per-MCP configuration.

Inspection runs inbound (catches an agent passing poisoned content to a tool) and outbound (catches an MCP returning content that would inject instructions into the agent's next turn). Latency impact is measured per route; low-risk paths skip inspection.

**Rate limiting and analytics.** Spike Arrest and Quota policies, keyed by `client_id`, prevent any single agent from overwhelming a backend. Apigee analytics with custom dimensions (`client_id`, `audience`, `tool_name`) provide per-agent and per-tool dashboards from day one, before downstream OpenTelemetry pickup is in place.

content:
### Layer 4: Identity, Authorization, and the Auth Request Workflow

Authentication and authorization use Duende IdentityServer, federated to Google IAM. The design has three structural guarantees and one defined process.

**Structural guarantee 1: MCP-as-resource, agent-as-client.** Each MCP is a distinct OAuth resource with its own audience. Each agent is registered as a Duende client with an explicit, bounded list of audiences it is allowed to request. An agent cannot obtain a token for a resource it was not provisioned for — Duende refuses to issue.

**Structural guarantee 2: Two-hop token exchange with downscoping.** A developer's Google identity is exchanged for an agent identity, which is exchanged for a resource-scoped MCP token. Each hop can narrow scopes but never widen them. The full delegation chain (human → agent → resource) is preserved in nested `act` claims and propagated through Apigee into MCP audit logs.

**Structural guarantee 3: Mode-separated clients.** Interactive (developer-in-the-loop) and autonomous modes are separate Duende clients with separate scope ceilings. The autonomous client is architecturally incapable of obtaining the broader scopes available to the interactive client.

**Process: the auth request workflow.** Every change to agent identity, scope, or audience binding flows through a defined request channel:

1. A requester (developer, team lead, platform engineer) files a request specifying the target MCPs, intended tools, mode (interactive or autonomous), and justification.
2. Requests are reviewed by an **approved users group**, a defined role with the Duende RBAC required to provision, modify, or revoke clients. Membership in the group and the RBAC role are kept in sync; removing a person from the group removes their Duende role.
3. Approved requests are executed against Duende. Resulting credentials are written into Apigee KVM through a privileged operator action with audit logging.
4. Revocations follow the same path in reverse: Duende client disabled, KVM entry removed. A periodic check flags orphaned KVM entries referring to deleted Duende clients.
5. Active agents undergo annual re-attestation by their owners through the same channel. Unattested agents are disabled.

To reduce review burden and keep scope sprawl in check, agents are provisioned against a small set of **agent profiles** (e.g., `scaffolding-readonly`, `scaffolding-readwrite`, `ticket-management`). Profiles define the scope/audience bundle. New agent requests pick a profile rather than designing bespoke scope sets per request.

### Layer 5: CI Enforcement

Architectural rules expressed in CLAUDE.md gain teeth only when CI enforces them. The platform ships:

- **Architecture tests** (NetArchTest or equivalent) that fail builds when layer boundaries are violated, when handlers carry side effects they shouldn't, or when controllers contain business logic.
- **Linter and formatter configurations** referenced directly from CLAUDE.md so the agent's verification commands and CI run the same checks.
- **PR checks** that flag agent-introduced code which appears to duplicate existing services, using the same Discovery MCP that the agent itself queries.

### Layer 6: Observability and Evaluation

- **Audit logging.** Every tool call logs a structured record: human identity, agent identity, MCP, tool name, arguments, result, duration, delegation chain. Apigee analytics provide the first-pass dashboard; structured logs are emitted in OpenTelemetry-compatible format for downstream pickup.
- **Evaluation suite.** A hand-curated set of representative tickets with rubric-based scoring (LLM-as-judge). Run weekly against the platform. Tracks whether changes to MCPs, prompts, or indexes improve or regress task outcomes.

---

## Phase 1: Pilot Scope

The pilot delivers a thin vertical slice of the architecture, end-to-end, used by a real developer on real tickets.

### Pilot Target

One developer, one service, one ticket type: **new CQRS command handlers in a designated C# service**. Success is measured over the first ten such tickets completed with the platform.

### Pilot Deliverables

The pilot scope depends on whether Apigee is already in production for the platform team. Two tracks are presented; pick one based on operational reality.

**Track A — Apigee already in production for the platform team:**

| Week | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| 1 | `CLAUDE.md` shipped to the target repository with exemplar pointers and verification commands. Baseline measured on next ticket. |
| 2 | CI architecture tests covering the CQRS layer boundary rules. |
| 3 | Duende client provisioned via the auth request workflow. Credentials placed in Apigee KVM. Single MCP proxy stood up in Apigee with VerifyJWT, rate limiting, and analytics. |
| 4–5 | Scaffolding MCP (CQRS command generation) and Discovery MCP (service/handler enumeration), deployed behind Apigee. Forwarded identity over mTLS to backends. |
| 6 | Audit logging end-to-end. 20-ticket eval suite drafted. Model Armor shared flow stubbed (off by default; enabled on Jira/Git MCPs in Phase 2). |
| 7–8 | Pilot developer uses the platform on real tickets. Eval suite run weekly. Findings documented. |

**Track B — Apigee net-new to the platform team:**

| Week | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| 1 | `CLAUDE.md` shipped to the target repository. Baseline measured on next ticket. |
| 2 | CI architecture tests covering the CQRS layer boundary rules. |
| 3–5 | Scaffolding MCP and Discovery MCP deployed locally with direct Duende JWT validation. Auth request workflow used to provision a single agent client with audience bindings. |
| 6 | Audit logging end-to-end. 20-ticket eval suite drafted. |
| 7–8 | Pilot developer uses the platform on real tickets. Eval suite run weekly. Findings documented. |
| Phase 1.5 | Apigee introduced as gateway in front of the existing MCPs. JWT validation migrates from per-MCP middleware to Apigee VerifyJWT policy. Forwarded identity over mTLS. Model Armor shared flow added. |

Both tracks produce the same eventual architecture. Track A pays the Apigee setup cost up front and avoids any later migration. Track B ships the pilot 2–3 weeks faster and pays the gateway-integration cost after the value is proven.

symbol: Explicitly Out of Scope for Phase 1
content:
### Explicitly Out of Scope for Phase 1

- Cross-repository pattern retrieval (pgvector).
- Jira and Git MCPs.
- Autonomous mode.
- Full Google IAM → Duende federation with two-hop token exchange.
- Re-attestation tooling (manual for Phase 1; automated in Phase 2).

These are Phase 2 items, prioritized based on what the pilot reveals.

### Success Criteria

The pilot is judged on three measurable outcomes over the ten-ticket window:

1. **Pattern adherence.** Percentage of PRs that pass architecture tests on the first run, without rework.
2. **Service reuse.** Number of new services created where an existing service would have sufficed (target: zero).
3. **Developer-reported friction.** Qualitative feedback on whether the platform sped up or slowed down the ticket.

If all three trend in the right direction, Phase 2 is justified. If not, the pilot has cheaply revealed that the thesis needs revision before more is built.

---

## Phase 2: Expansion

Phase 2 work is sequenced based on pilot findings. Candidate scope includes:

- **Cross-repository pattern retrieval.** pgvector with commit-hash-keyed embeddings, on-demand hotfix indexing, semantic chunking with role metadata (service / controller / test / fixture).
- **Jira and Git MCPs** behind Apigee with Model Armor enabled on inbound arguments and outbound results.
- **Full federated identity.** Google IAM → Duende → MCP with two-hop token exchange and full `act` chain propagation through Apigee.
- **Autonomous mode.** Separate Duende client, narrower scope ceiling, integrated with scheduled tasks for tickets that fit a known pattern.
- **Automated re-attestation tooling** integrated with the auth request channel.
- **Broader pilot.** Expansion from one developer/one service to a team/multiple services.

---

## Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Standards rot.** `CLAUDE.md`, scaffolding templates, and exemplar files go stale and start misleading the agent. | Named owner per repository. Quarterly review cadence. Treat these artifacts as production code with deprecation processes. |
| **Pattern enforcement is too weak.** Retrieval alone allows the agent to ignore patterns it should follow. | Layered defenses: prompt guidance, scaffolding tools (correct-by-construction), CI architecture tests (the actual teeth). |
| **Embedding-based retrieval underperforms grep.** | Build the homegrown eval suite first. If embeddings don't measurably beat grep on real queries, downscope or remove the pgvector layer. |
| **Auth request channel becomes a bottleneck.** | Agent profiles reduce per-request review effort to "is this agent legitimate" rather than "are these scopes correctly designed." Standard profiles handle the common cases. |
| **Apigee KVM and Duende client list drift after revocation.** | Periodic orphan-check job flags KVM entries referring to deleted Duende clients. Revocation runbook makes KVM cleanup unmissable. |
| **Approved users group erodes through informal approvals.** | Duende RBAC is the structural gate, not the channel. Only group members have the role; non-members are technically incapable of provisioning. |
| **Project sprawl without a real user.** | Pilot is scoped to one developer, one ticket type, one service. No additional infrastructure is built until the pilot demonstrates value. |
| **Audit trail attributes agent actions to humans alone.** | Structured audit logging with full delegation chain from day one. Apigee forwards delegation context; MCPs log it. |
| **Model Armor adds unacceptable latency on interactive paths.** | Per-MCP risk-weighted policy. Low-risk paths (Discovery on internal code) skip inspection. High-risk paths (Jira ticket content, Git messages) are inspected and fail closed. |

---

## Industry Context

This design is consistent with where the enterprise MCP ecosystem has converged in 2026:

- **MCP is the de facto standard.** Adopted by every major vendor; ~10,000 active servers in the public registry; supported by Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Copilot, and others.
- **AGENTS.md** is the open standard for agent behavior guidance, used by 60,000+ repositories.
- **Workflow-shaped tools** outperform API-wrapping tools when consumed by agents. Multiple major vendors have published on this independently.
- **Enterprise MCP gateways** (Apigee, Google Agent Gateway, Cloudflare MCP Server Portal, Kong AI Gateway, open-source `agentgateway`) are the standard pattern for governance at scale. This platform uses Apigee.
- **Resource-scoped OAuth with two-hop delegation** is the pattern endorsed by the MCP authorization specification (OAuth 2.1 with resource indicators per RFC 8707, protected resource metadata per RFC 9728).
- **Manual client provisioning with profile-based scope bundling** is the standard pattern when agent counts are small enough to be managed by a defined human workflow rather than DCR. DCR is appropriate at much larger scale and at the cost of significant operational complexity.

The platform does not depart from industry direction; it adopts it deliberately and applies it to this organization's specific patterns.

---

## Open Questions for Stakeholders

1. **First pilot user and service.** Who is the developer, and which service is the pilot target?
2. **Apigee track selection.** Is Apigee already in production for the platform team (Track A) or net-new (Track B)?
3. **Ownership of `CLAUDE.md` and scaffolding templates.** Which team owns these artifacts long-term?
4. **Composition of the approved users group** for the auth request workflow, and the channel it operates through (Jira project, Slack channel, ticket queue).
5. **Eval rubric authorship.** Who writes the rubric for "did this PR follow our pattern"? This shapes the entire feedback loop.
6. **Phase 2 trigger.** What pilot result justifies investment in Phase 2? What result would cause us to revise the thesis?

---

## Appendix: Decision Log

Key architectural decisions made during design, with the alternative considered:

| Decision | Alternative Considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Consume existing agents (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) | Build proprietary agent | Agent loop is commoditized; differentiation is in the MCPs and patterns. |
| Workflow-shaped tools | API-wrapping tools | Workflow tools produce reliable agent behavior; API tools require the agent to compose correctly. |
| Roslyn for service discovery | Embedding-based discovery | Precision matters more than recall for canonical service lookup; AST is exact. |
| pgvector for cross-repo retrieval only | pgvector for everything | Single-repo retrieval is well-served by grep + Roslyn; cross-repo is the legitimate embedding use case. |
| MCP-as-resource, audience-bound | Single shared audience across MCPs | Resource isolation is the strongest structural guardrail against token replay. |
| Apigee as MCP gateway | Per-MCP auth middleware indefinitely | Centralized JWT validation, rate limiting, Model Armor, and analytics. Backend MCPs simplified to trust forwarded identity over mTLS. |
| Manual client provisioning via auth request workflow | Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) | DCR introduces a second source of truth (Apigee templates vs Duende state) and creates drift/reconciliation problems. At expected agent counts, a defined manual process with profiles is cleaner and auditable. |
| Duende is single source of truth for identity | Split source of truth between Apigee and Duende | Eliminates drift, reconciliation, and the ambiguity of which system grants privilege. Apigee KVM holds cached operational state, not authoritative state. |
| Approved users group with Duende RBAC | Open provisioning channel with social approval | RBAC enforces the gate structurally; the channel is the workflow. Membership in the group and the RBAC role stay synchronized. |
| Agent profiles (scope bundles) | Bespoke scope sets per agent | Profiles make per-request review tractable and prevent scope sprawl across dozens of similar agents. |
| Model Armor per-MCP, risk-weighted | Model Armor on every request | Latency budget matters for interactive use. Internal codebase content is low-risk; external content (Jira, Git messages) is high-risk. Inspection effort follows risk. |
| CLAUDE.md + CI tests + scaffolding tools (layered) | Embeddings + prompt alone | Prose guidance is necessary but insufficient; structural patterns require structural enforcement. |

parentSymbol: Proposal — Decommissioning the .NET Monolith into Federated Web Modules
content:
## 1. Summary

Decompose the current full-stack `Rxo.Platform.Web.Sandbox` (.NET monolith + MVC) into:

- A **slim .NET shell** that owns first-byte HTML, global navigation, theme, and the encrypted-cookie auth handshake.
- **Independently-deployed federated web modules** (already-existing `<web_sandbox_mfe>` Custom Element pattern) loaded by manifest, one per page / page-group.
- **Apigee** as the edge gateway — decrypts the .NET-issued cookie, validates the session, and forwards a trusted identity header to:
- A **.NET BFF** (re-using `src/api/`) that exposes an OpenAPI contract from which the frontends auto-generate strongly-typed TypeScript clients (matching `src/frontend/src/clients/` conventions).

The first stage is a **POC**: lift one low-friction page (recommended: the `Index` landing page in `src/frontend/src/pages/index.tsx`, which has no data dependencies) out of the monolith and serve it as a standalone federated web module.

parentSymbol: Proposal — Decommissioning the .NET Monolith into Federated Web Modules
content:
## 2. Motivation

| Pain point today | What this proposal fixes |
|---|---|
| Pages, providers, routes, auth flow, and SSR all ship as one bundle — every change rebuilds + redeploys everything. | Per-module independent deploys via `manifest.json`. |
| Cookie crosses Apigee directly to the BFF — one auth chain, one runtime. |
| Two runtimes (Node + .NET) in the request path → two sets of dependencies, two CVE surfaces, two log streams to correlate. | One runtime (.NET) at the edge of the platform; UI ships as static assets from a CDN/asset bucket. |
| Hand-written API clients in `src/frontend/src/clients/` drift from server contracts. | Generated TS clients from the BFF's OpenAPI doc — contract is the source of truth. |
| Each new feature touches entire monolith in lockstep — high cognitive cost for AI agents and humans. | One contract (BFF) + one UI module. AI agents driven by `codemcp` patterns produce predictable scaffolds. |
| `Web Component` pattern (`src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx`) is built but never exercised in production. | It becomes the **default** delivery mechanism. |

parentSymbol: Proposal — Decommissioning the .NET Monolith into Federated Web Modules
content: ## 3. Scope

### In scope

- Producing the target architecture diagram, contracts, and migration stages.
- Defining the .NET-encrypted-cookie ↔ Apigee ↔ BFF auth handshake.
- Defining the manifest-based loader contract that the .NET shell will use to mount remote modules.
- Defining the OpenAPI → TypeScript client generation pipeline and where the generated code lives.
- Defining the POC: replace the `Index` page with a federated web module loaded from a static asset host.
- Defining how `codemcp` is used to standardize each migration.

### Out of scope

- Replacing **SQL** or any persistence in `src/api/Repository/`. The BFF re-uses the existing repository layer.
- Replacing the existing **gRPC** inter-service traffic in `src/api/Services/Proto`.
- Migration of `src/test/` Cypress tests (they continue to target the running monolith during transition; new modules ship with their own Cypress specs side-by-side).
- Changing the **MUI theme / brand** — the shell continues to own theme tokens.
- Adopting a different micro-frontend framework (Module Federation, single-spa, etc.). We use the **already-working** `<web_sandbox_mfe>` Custom Element + `manifest.json` pattern; no new abstraction.

parentSymbol: Proposal — Decommissioning the .NET Monolith into Federated Web Modules
content: ## 5. Architectural pillars

### 5.1 The shell — what stays in .NET

The shell is the **only** monolith descendant. It owns:

- **First-byte HTML** — a minimal `index.html` that mounts the global chrome (header / nav / footer / theme root) and a `<div id="region-…">` per page region.
- **Routing** — server-side route → manifest mapping. Each route resolves to `{ moduleId, manifestUrl, basePath }` and emits a `<script>` block that calls `window.__loadManifest__(manifestUrl, moduleId, callback)` followed by `window.__initialize_web_component(id, basePath, accessToken, user, dataContext)`. Both helpers already exist in [`src/frontend/src/public/manifest.33120261.js`](../src/frontend/src/public/manifest.33120261.js).
- **Bootstrap context** — minted server-side: the user identity, runtime config (`appsettings.json` per env), basePath, and a short-lived access token (decrypted from the cookie). Passed into each web module via the `initialize` `CustomEvent` defined in [`src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx`](../src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx) (`IInitializeEventDetail`).
- **Cookie minting + refresh** — re-uses `Rxo.Auth.Authentication` already wired in [`src/backend/Host/Program.cs`](../src/backend/Host/Program.cs) (`AddRxoAuthCookieAuthentication`, `AddRxoRefreshTokenService`).

What the shell **does not** own:

- Page-specific data fetching.
- Page-specific UI logic.
- Any business endpoints (they all move to the BFF).

symbol: 5.2 Web modules — what each page becomes
content:
### 5.2 Web modules — what each page becomes

Each "page" (or coherent page-group) becomes a federated module that:

1. Ships its own Webpack build with two outputs — a `web_component.js` entry (already produced by [`src/frontend/webpack.config.mjs`](../src/frontend/webpack.config.mjs) for `<web_sandbox_mfe>`) and an emitted `manifest.json` (already produced by `WebpackManifestPlugin`).
2. Defines a Custom Element tag (`<rxo-{module}-mfe>`).
3. Receives bootstrap state via the `initialize` `CustomEvent` — no global imports of `UserContext`, no PKCE flow inside the module. The pattern is exactly [`src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx`](../src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx) (lines 89–129).
4. Talks to the BFF **only** via auto-generated clients (see §5.4) — never directly to `src/backend/` or `src/api/`.
5. Is deployed to a static asset host (CDN/bucket); the shell references it by manifest URL.

content:
#### Module loader contract

This already exists — we just elevate it from "internal helper" to "platform-level contract":

| Helper | File | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `window.__loadManifest__(path, entry, cb)` | [`manifest.33120261.js`](../src/frontend/src/public/manifest.33120261.js) lines 53–95 | Fetches a remote `manifest.json`, resolves vendor + entry chunks, injects `<script>` tags. |
| `window.__loadAssets__(asset, cb)` | same file, lines 2–32 | Idempotent script/CSS injector. |
| `window.__initialize_web_component(id, basepath, accessToken, user, data)` | same file, lines 33–52 | Waits for the Custom Element to report `ready="true"`, then dispatches the `initialize` `CustomEvent`. |

Migration steps reuse these unchanged.

### 5.3 Authentication — encrypted cookie → Apigee → BFF ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant S as .NET shell participant A as Apigee participant F as .NET BFF B->>S: GET / (no cookie) S->>S: AddRxoAuthCookieAuthentication challenge → IdP PKCE S-->>B: 200 HTML + Set-Cookie: rxo_session=...encrypted... B->>A: GET /bff/v1/weather (cookie attached) A->>A: Decrypt cookie with shared key, validate, extract claims A->>F: GET /v1/weather
+ x-rxo-user: {sub, email, scopes} F->>F: Trust header (network-level mTLS to Apigee) F-->>A: 200 weather payload A-->>B: 200 weather payload ``` Key points: - The cookie is **opaque to JavaScript** (`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`) — no token leakage to web modules. - The shell continues to own cookie issuance using **the existing `Rxo.Auth` packages** — no new identity stack. We expose the **decryption key** to Apigee via a shared KMS secret. - The BFF authenticates **the Apigee channel** (mTLS or signed JWT issued by Apigee), not the user — trust is delegated. This is a one-way change: the BFF must reject requests that arrive without the Apigee-asserted identity header. - The short-lived in-page `accessToken` passed through `IInitializeEventDetail` is **optional** — kept for cases where a web module needs to call a non-Apigee third-party API directly. Most calls go cookie-only.

### 5.4 BFF contract & client generation

- The BFF lives in `src/api/` (already structured Domain → Repository → Services → Host per [`src/api/CLAUDE.md`](../src/api/CLAUDE.md)). We **do not** create a new project — we add BFF-specific endpoints alongside existing ones, scoped under `/bff/v1/...`.
- Endpoints return **UI-shaped models** (`*ViewModel`), not raw `*Entity` or `*Dto`. Following the existing convention in `src/backend/Services/`, `ViewModels` go in `src/api/Services/Models/ViewModels/`.
- OpenAPI is already emitted by `AddSwaggerGen` (see `src/backend/Host/Program.cs` line 77 — we replicate this in `src/api/Host`).
- **Client generation pipeline:**
  1. CI builds the BFF, runs it locally, fetches `/swagger/v1/swagger.json`.
  2. `nswag` or `openapi-typescript-codegen` emits TS clients into a versioned npm package `@rxo/platform-bff-client`.
  3. Each web module consumes the package; clients follow the shape already used in [`src/frontend/src/clients/useWeatherClient.ts`](../src/frontend/src/clients/useWeatherClient.ts) — a hook returning `IUseWeatherClientResult` per the type-conventions in [`CLAUDE.BASE.md`](../CLAUDE.BASE.md).

### 5.5 codemcp-driven standardization

Every migration follows the workspace rule in [`CLAUDE.md`](../CLAUDE.md): **discovery via `codemcp` only, no `Glob` / `Grep` / `Read` fallback**. Concretely, each new web module is scaffolded by an agent that:

1. Runs `mcp__codemcp__get_file_context` on `src/frontend/src/web_module/web_module.tsx` and the page being lifted.
2. Runs `mcp__codemcp__search_code` with `area: "frontend"` for `manifest`, `IInitializeEventDetail`, and the page's domain concept.
3. Runs `mcp__codemcp__find_symbol` for the matching `useXxxClient` to mirror its shape.
4. Produces the new module with **no new abstractions** — same providers, same client convention, same manifest plugin output.

This keeps each migration mechanically similar so reviews and rollbacks are predictable.

content:
## 6. Migration stages

Each stage ships independently and is reversible.

### Stage 0 — Baseline (no code changes)

- Document the auth handshake, the manifest contract, and the BFF contract (this proposal).
- Confirm Apigee proxy availability in the target environment.
- Confirm static asset host (bucket + CDN) is provisioned.

symbol: Stage 1 — POC: Lift the Index page
content:
### Stage 1 — POC: Lift the Index page

Replace one low-friction page with a federated module. Recommended target: [`src/frontend/src/pages/index.tsx`](../src/frontend/src/pages/index.tsx) — currently a static `<Box>` + `<Typography>`, no data fetching, no permissions.

Deliverables:

- New build entry under `src/frontend/` (or a new sibling folder) producing `index_mfe.js` + `manifest.json` registered as `<rxo-index-mfe>`.
- Static UI only — no BFF calls in this stage.
- Shell change in [`src/backend/Host/Program.cs`](../src/backend/Host/Program.cs): on `GET /` and `GET /home/index`, render an HTML page that loads the module via `__loadManifest__` and dispatches `initialize` via `__initialize_web_component`.
- Cypress smoke test verifying `/` still renders "Welcome to Platform Sandbox Web".

Exit criteria for Stage 1:

- Index page is served by the new module in `local` and `dev` environments.
- The monolith bundle no longer contains `pages/index.tsx`.
- Rollback is a single config flip (route registration in the shell).

### Stage 2 — BFF foundation

- Stand up `/bff/v1/...` route group in `src/api/Host`.
- Wire Apigee in front of the BFF (mTLS or signed JWT trust).
- Add the OpenAPI → TS client pipeline; publish `@rxo/platform-bff-client@0.0.1` (initially exporting one stub endpoint).
- No web module consumes it yet — this stage proves the pipeline only.

Exit criteria for Stage 2:

- `@rxo/platform-bff-client` installable from the npm feed.
- Apigee successfully forwards a request from the browser to `/bff/v1/ping` and returns 200.
- BFF rejects the same request when called directly (bypassing Apigee).

### Stage 3 — Lift a data-bearing page (Weather)

Repeat Stage 1 for [`src/frontend/src/pages/weather.tsx`](../src/frontend/src/pages/weather.tsx), now using `@rxo/platform-bff-client` for data. This is the first **real** exercise of the end-to-end auth + contract chain.

- New module `<rxo-weather-mfe>`.
- Replace `useWeatherClient` with the generated client.

### Stage 4 — Lift remaining pages

One page (or page-group) per PR. Each follows the codemcp-driven scaffold.

### Stage 5 — Slim the .NET monolith

- Strip `src/backend/Host/Program.cs` to only the shell concerns (auth, route → manifest, asset middleware).
- Remove `src/backend/Services/Endpoints/` once all endpoints have moved to the BFF.
- Optionally rename to `src/shell/`.

- [ ] Apigee KMS key sharing model is signed off by security.
- [ ] Static asset hosting topology is signed off by SRE (CORS, cache headers, version pinning).

content:
## 8. Open questions

- **Apigee crypto model**: do we hand Apigee the .NET DataProtection key directly, or do we move cookie issuance to a Rxo.Auth.Edge service that both .NET and Apigee call? The latter is cleaner but adds a hop in the cookie-mint path.
- **Module-to-module shared state**: today everything lives in `UserContext` / `ApplicationContext` in the same React tree. In the federated world, each module has its own React tree inside its own Shadow DOM (per `web_module.tsx` line 90). For cross-module state (e.g. notifications), do we use `CustomEvent` bubbling on `window`, a shared `BroadcastChannel`, or a small global store loaded by the shell?
- **SSR**: do we still need any HTML pre-rendering for SEO / first-paint? Today's Monolith is the only thing producing meaningful first HTML. Possible answers: (a) accept fully-CSR for authenticated app, (b) keep a minimal Razor pre-render in the shell, (c) per-module pre-render at build time and cache.
- **Generated client style**: NSwag (.NET-tooling-aligned) vs `openapi-typescript-codegen` (TS-native, simpler). Tied to whichever produces hooks that mirror [`useWeatherClient.ts`](../src/frontend/src/clients/useWeatherClient.ts) most cleanly.
- **Cypress strategy**: keep `src/test/` as the umbrella suite hitting the deployed shell, or move per-page tests inside each module's repo/folder? Recommend the former during transition (Stages 1–4) and revisit at Stage 5.

## 10. Notes for AI agents

- **No new abstractions.** Reuse `<web_sandbox_mfe>`, `__loadManifest__`, `__initialize_web_component`, and the existing `useXxxClient` shape verbatim. If a stage seems to require a new wrapper, stop and surface the gap.
- **Discovery via codemcp only.** Before lifting any page, `get_file_context` the page + its current client + `web_module.tsx`. Do not `Glob`/`Grep` for analogous patterns.
- **One stage per PR.** Stages are intentionally small and independently reversible — do not bundle them.
- **Do not touch the gRPC inter-service path** in `src/api/Services/Proto` as part of these stages — it is explicitly out of scope.
- **Generated clients are generated, not hand-edited.** If a client is wrong, fix the BFF contract or the generator template — never the emitted file.

## node-express-ssr (src/frontend/src/server)

Canonical: `src/frontend/src/server/server.tsx` + middleware (`oidc_auth.ts`, `user_context.ts`, `api_proxy.tsx`, `ssr_render.tsx`).

- This is the **Node backend that hosts the React app** — not a generic Node API. It packages with `src/frontend` and exists to provide SSR + auth + API tunneling for [[frontend-sandbox]].
- Middleware order is load-bearing — config → logger → OIDC → userContext → apiProxy → static → SSR. Each step writes onto `req` for downstream consumers; reordering silently breaks identity, proxy headers, or static caching.
- Authentication via `express-openid-connect` with `authRequired: false`. SSR must render anonymous shells; route-level authorization is enforced in React via `userContext` and `AuthorizedRoute` ([[frontend-sandbox]]). Scopes list every API audience the frontend calls (`openid email name xpo-auth-api rxo-platform-api-sandbox`) — adding an audience requires updating both the scope list and the IDP client registration.
- `userContextMiddleware` resolves identity + permissions **once per request** (parallel `Promise.all`) and attaches `req.userContext = { accessToken, userInfo, permissions }`. Anonymous shape is `{ accessToken: null, userInfo: null, permissions: [] }` — never `undefined`. Downstream middleware reads from `req.userContext`; never refetch from the IDP or permissions service.
- `apiProxyMiddleware` intercepts `/api/*` and tunnels to `req.serverConfig["api-address"]` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` + `x-signature: <HMAC>`. Streams in/out via `pipeline()` + `duplex: 'half'` — do not buffer bodies. Replaced the legacy `rxo_ssit` shared encrypted cookie ([[project_api_proxy_refactoring]]).
- Frontend Axios `baseUrl: '/api'` always — never call the .NET API origin directly from the browser. The access token never reaches the client: SSR redacts it to `'AccessTokenHidden'` before serializing state into HTML and escapes `<` to prevent `</script>` injection.
- SSR uses `renderToPipeableStream` wrapped in the **exact same provider stack** as the client (`ApplicationContextProvider → UserContextProvider → AxiosContextProvider → NotificationContextProvider → ErrorBoundary → AppStart → Layout → RouteConfig`). Any change to provider order, nesting, or `value` shape must be mirrored on both sides or hydration mismatches.
- `onShellReady` flushes the head and starts streaming; `onError` redirects to `/error` only if headers aren't yet sent — once the shell is flushed, log only. `ssrRenderMiddleware` redirects bare paths into `basePath` and short-circuits `/public`/`/assets` to `next()`.
- Secrets (`secret`, `clientSecret`, signing keys) live in `appsettings.json` — never log `req.serverConfig` wholesale.

## docker-image (src/api/Dockerfile, src/frontend/Dockerfile)

Canonical: `src/api/Dockerfile` (.NET flavor) and `src/frontend/Dockerfile` (Node flavor). Both are multi-stage with public SDK build → internal RXO runtime base.

- **Always two stages.** Public SDK image (`mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0` for .NET, `node:22-slim` for Node) builds; internal `$BASE_IMAGE` (`nxo-baseimage-net-core8` or `nxo-baseimage-nodejs22`) runs. Never ship an SDK image as the runtime.
- **`ARG BASE_IMAGE` + `ARG BUILD_CONTEXT` injected by the pipeline** via `--build-arg`. Declare `ARG BASE_IMAGE` before the first `FROM $BASE_IMAGE` and re-declare `ARG BUILD_CONTEXT` after each `FROM` that uses it (Docker ARG scoping is per-stage). No hardcoded base images — that bypasses pipeline-driven version pinning.
- **Final `WORKDIR /application`** across all containers in this repo.
- **.NET flavor (`src/api/Dockerfile`)**: build with `dotnet/sdk:8.0` → `dotnet clean && dotnet restore && dotnet publish -c Release -o out`; copy `$BUILD_CONTEXT/out` into `/application`; install `libicu72`; set `DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=true`; listen on `:8080` via `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS=8080` and `ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080`. Keep both the invariant flag and `libicu72` — culture-aware libraries probe for ICU at startup even with the flag on. Pipeline passes `BUILD_CONTEXT=src/api/Host/Rxo.Platform.Api.Sandbox.Host`.
- **Node flavor (`src/frontend/Dockerfile`)**: build with `node:22-slim` → `npm ci && node clean.mjs && webpack --config webpack.prod.mjs --mode=production`. Webpack emits three trees with **different deployment targets**:
  - `publish/` → container `/application/` (compiled Express SSR — see [[node-express-ssr]]).
  - `dist/public/` → container `./public` — user-loadable content (`index.html`, favicons, manifests). Served by Express.
  - `dist/static/` → **NOT in the container** — hashed webpack chunks, served by Firebase Hosting as the CDN ([[firebase-hosting]] chunk-CDN shape). SSR-emitted HTML references them via absolute Firebase URLs. Do not re-add the `COPY dist/static ./public/static` line.
  Runtime stage copies `node_modules`, `publish/`, `dist/public` only. `npm ci` only — never `npm install` in CI. Build-env Node major must match runtime base major (22 ↔ 22). `PORT=80` default for local runs; Cloud Run overrides. Pipeline passes `BUILD_CONTEXT=src/frontend`.
- **`libicu72` + `DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=true` on both flavors** — the Node base also carries dotnet shared tooling.
- **Copy order in the runtime stage favors cache**: `node_modules` first (least churn), then app output, then static assets. Reordering hurts incremental rebuilds.
- **No secrets in image layers.** `--build-arg` only for non-sensitive params (paths, base image refs).
- **Pipeline wiring**: `dockerFilePath` is the directory (template looks for `Dockerfile` inside); `buildContext: '.'` is the repo root so `COPY . ./` sees siblings (multi-project .NET solution, shared frontend modules). `BASE_IMAGE` bumps are deliberate and isolated commits — never part of an unrelated change.
- **Legacy Dockerfile at `src/api/Host/.../Dockerfile`** (.NET 6, raw `mcr.microsoft.com` runtime) is a VS-scaffolded debug-only file the pipeline does not use — do not maintain it as production. The `src/backend/Dockerfile` is older (.NET 6 + the legacy `nxo-baseimage-dotnet-core` line) and not the canonical pattern.

## webpack (src/frontend/webpack.*.mjs)

Canonical: `src/frontend/webpack.config.mjs` (base, exports `[clientConfig, serverConfig]`), `webpack.dev.mjs` + `webpack.prod.mjs` (overlays via `webpack-merge`).

- **Three-file split** — base + dev + prod. Base defines both configs; dev/prod re-export `[client, server]` after `merge` with mode-flipped output naming and stats. Loaders/plugins live in the base, not in dev/prod.
- **Two configs per run** — base factory returns `[clientConfig, serverConfig]`; single `webpack` invocation produces both. They share `resolve.extensions` and the babel rule; everything else diverges.
- **`clientConfig`** (browser):
  - Target = default (`web`).
  - Entry: `{ app: 'src/client/entry.tsx', web_component: 'src/web_module/web_module.tsx' }`. Sub-routes use `@loadable/component` chunks ([[frontend-sandbox]]); they do not need additional entry points.
  - Output: `dist/static/` with hashed `[name].[fullhash].js` / `[name].[chunkhash].js`. `output.publicPath: './dist/static'` is the dev fallback; runtime URLs resolve through the manifest plugin's `publicPath: '/rxo-platform-web-sandbox/public/static'`.
  - Loaders: babel + json + css + (xpo svg) + file-loader.
  - Plugins: `MiniCssExtractPlugin`, `WebpackManifestPlugin`, `ProvidePlugin($/jQuery)`, `CopyPlugin` (stages `src/public/*` → `dist/public/*` for the container's `./public`).
  - `optimization.splitChunks` required (vendors + shared default groups).
  - `watchOptions: { poll: 1000, ignored: /node_modules/ }` — required for Docker-Desktop / WSL2 dev.
  - Consumed by Firebase Hosting CDN ([[firebase-hosting]] chunk-CDN shape).
- **`serverConfig`** (SSR):
  - `target: 'node'` + `externals: [nodeExternals()]` — every `node_modules` import stays external. The Docker runtime image carries `./node_modules` separately ([[docker-image]] Node flavor).
  - Entry: `src/server/server.tsx`. Output: `publish/index.js` — filename is fixed (both Dockerfile and Express expect that entrypoint name).
  - Loaders: babel + `empty-loader.js` for `(css|svg|jpg|jpeg|png|gif|mp3)` — SSR never embeds assets.
  - Plugins: `CopyPlugin` only — stages `appsettings.json`, `appsettings.release.json`, SSR `index.html` (the lodash-templated shell consumed by `flushBody` in [[node-express-ssr]]), and `src/public/*` (local-dev convenience; production `./public` comes from `dist/public/` via the Dockerfile).
  - No `optimization.splitChunks`, no `WebpackManifestPlugin`, no `MiniCssExtractPlugin`, no `ProvidePlugin`. Adding any of these is a smell — the server is a single `index.js` against a controlled runtime.
  - Server stays mostly untouched between dev/prod — only `mode` flips. Do not add `TerserPlugin` overrides.
  - Consumed by Express SSR container ([[node-express-ssr]], [[docker-image]] Node flavor).
- **Loaders:**
  - `babel-loader` with `@babel/preset-env` + `@babel/preset-react` — **required**, universal across JS/JSX/TS/TSX (no TypeScript preset; type-checking is the IDE/`tsc --noEmit` job).
  - `MiniCssExtractPlugin.loader` + `css-loader` for `.css` — **optional** (only fires if CSS files exist; rule stays in as a no-op safety net so future stylesheet imports don't require touching webpack).
  - `@svgr/webpack` + the repo's `log-loader.js` for `.svg` — **optional, gated by `include: [.../@xpo/icons]`**. Path-gated, not extension-gated. Generic SVGs fall through to file-loader.
  - `file-loader` (`[path][name]-[hash:8].[ext]`) for `.jpg|.jpeg|.png|.gif|.mp3|.svg` from the app source tree (`exclude: node_modules`) — **required**.
  - `json-loader` for `.json` — required, client only, excludes `node_modules`.
  - Server config short-circuits all `(css|svg|jpg|jpeg|png|gif|mp3)` via `empty-loader.js` — SSR never embeds assets.
- **Plugins:**
  - `MiniCssExtractPlugin` — pairs with the CSS rule; emits `[name].css` / `[id].css`.
  - `WebpackManifestPlugin` — **required**. `publicPath: "/rxo-platform-web-sandbox/public/static"` — SSR HTML resolves chunk URLs through `manifest.json` against the Firebase Hosting origin. Drift between `publicPath`, SSR template, and Firebase site name breaks chunk loads in the browser.
  - `webpack.ProvidePlugin({ $: 'jquery', jQuery: 'jquery' })` — **optional**. Polyfills bare `$`/`jQuery` references in legacy modules; drop in lockstep with `jquery` being removed from `package.json`.
  - `CopyPlugin` — required. Client stages `src/public/*` (index.html template, favicons, `manifest.33120261.js`, `appsettings.json`) into `dist/public/` (which becomes the container's `./public`). Server stages `appsettings.json`, `appsettings.release.json`, SSR `index.html`, and `src/public/*` into `publish/`.
- **Chunkification — required** via `optimization.splitChunks`:
  - `chunks: 'all'`, `defaultVendors` group (`/node_modules/` → `vendors` chunk, priority `-10`), `default` group (`minChunks: 4`, priority `-20`), `reuseExistingChunk: true` on both.
  - Without it the manifest plugin produces a monolithic bundle; with it the manifest emits one URL per chunk and Firebase Hosting can cache vendors separately from app code.
  - `@loadable/component` produces additional `chunk_[domain]_[component]` chunks at runtime ([[frontend-sandbox]]) — no `magic comment` needed, the loadable plugin owns naming.
- **Server config never minifies.** Server `serverConfig` only flips `mode` between dev/prod; do not add `TerserPlugin` overrides — the SSR bundle ships to a controlled runtime, not a CDN.
- **Hashed output names in both modes** (`[name].[fullhash].js`, `[name].[chunkhash].js`) — long-lived dev watch sessions need cache busting too.
- **Performance budgets**: `hints: false`, `maxEntrypointSize: 400000`, `maxAssetSize: 300000` — track in PR review, not at build time.

# codeindex

Repository vectorizer. Walks a working tree, chunks it semantically, embeds the chunks, and publishes them to either PostgreSQL/pgvector or a local file directory. The output is consumed by [codemcp](../../src/codemcp/), which exposes it to coding assistants via the Model Context Protocol.

## Build

```bash
cd tools/codeindex
npm install
npm run build
```

Produces `dist/cli.js`.

## Invocation

```
node dist/cli.js [global-options] <command>
```

The **directory being indexed** defaults to `process.cwd()`. Pass **`--root <path>`** to index another folder (path is resolved relative to cwd when relative). There is no environment-variable fallback for the tree root; other settings are CLI flags or the optional config file.

### Global options

| Flag | Default | Source priority | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-r, --root <path>` | `cwd` | CLI | Directory to walk for indexing. Config file defaults to `<root>/codeindex.config.json` when `-c` is omitted. |
| `-c, --config <path>` | `<root>/codeindex.config.json` | CLI | Path to the config file (resolved relative to cwd). |
| `-b, --backend <pg\|file>` | `pg` | CLI | Storage backend. |
| `--branch <name>` | `main` | CLI | Branch name recorded on the commit row. |
| `--embed-provider <local\|voyage\|openai>` | `local` | CLI | Embedding model provider. |
| `--embed-dim <n>` | `768` | CLI | Embedding dimensionality (must match `chunks.embedding` for pg backend). |
| `--repository <name>` | (auto-detect) | CLI | Override for the repository id on the commit row. When omitted: `owner/repo` from `remote.origin.url` if available, otherwise the **resolved absolute path** of the index root (forward slashes). Multi-repo backends filter by this string plus `branch`. |

The file backend always reads/writes `tools/codeindex/data/` (next to the binary). There is no `--file-dir` flag — keep it simple, predictable, and cwd-independent.

Only `connectionString` and `excludeGlobs` live in the optional `codeindex.config.json`:

```json
{
  "connectionString": "postgres://codeindex_user:CHANGE_ME@localhost:5432/codeindex",
  "excludeGlobs": [
    "**/node_modules/**",
    "**/dist/**",
    "**/bin/**",
    "**/obj/**",
    "**/publish/**",
    "**/.git/**"
  ]
}
```

The config file is optional — built-in defaults cover both fields when it's absent.
## Commands

### `plan`

Walks the working tree and prints the file list without touching the backend. Use this to sanity-check what would be indexed before running `publish`.

```bash
cd <repo-root>
node tools/codeindex/dist/cli.js plan
```

Output begins with a context block (root dir, backend, branch, embed provider/dim) so you can see exactly what would happen.

### `migrate`

Applies pending SQL migrations from [migrations/](./migrations/) to the configured backend.

| Backend | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `pg` | Executes each `.sql` script in a transaction, then records it in `schema_versions`. Forward-only; checksums are verified against the journal on every run. Uses a Postgres advisory lock so concurrent runs serialize. |
| `file` | Skips SQL execution (file backend has no schema engine), records the same migration name + checksum in `<file-dir>/schema_versions.json`. Keeps the journal in lockstep with what Postgres would have. |

```bash

# apply
node tools/codeindex/dist/cli.js --backend pg migrate
node tools/codeindex/dist/cli.js --backend file migrate

# status (no changes)
node tools/codeindex/dist/cli.js --backend pg migrate --status
```

### `publish`

Runs migrations first, then walks → chunks → embeds → writes the current commit. Idempotent at the commit-SHA level.

```bash

# Postgres
cd <repo-root>
node tools/codeindex/dist/cli.js --backend pg publish
```

### Multi-repository indexes

Every commit is tagged with a `repository` identifier (`owner/repo` from `origin` when present, otherwise the resolved absolute path of the index root, or an explicit `--repository` override). A single backend can therefore hold commits from many repos; the [codemcp](../../tools/codemcp/) reader scopes its `latest commit for branch` lookup to `(repository, branch)` so two clones with overlapping branch names (e.g. both have a `main`) don't collide when they use distinct repository ids.

The Postgres `repository` column is **NOT NULL** with no default — every publish must produce one. The supporting migration is [migrations/002_add_repository.sql](./migrations/002_add_repository.sql). Existing pre-002 commits must be re-published (the migration sets them to an empty string, which the reader treats as "no repository" and excludes from repo-filtered queries).

## What gets indexed

The walker honors `.gitignore` at the cwd plus the `excludeGlobs` from the config (or the defaults: `node_modules`, `dist`, `bin`, `obj`, `publish`, `.git`). Indexable extensions: `.cs`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.md`, `.sql`, `.proto`, `.json`, `.yml`, `.yaml`. Files over 512 KB are skipped.

### Chunking

| File type | Chunker | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `.cs` | brace-depth + regex header detection | class, record, interface, method |
| `.ts` / `.tsx` / `.js` / `.jsx` | brace-depth + regex header detection | function, class, interface, React component |
| `.md` | header-level walk | sections (preserves nesting) |
| `.sql` | statement splitter (string/dollar-quote aware) | individual statements with object names |
| `.proto` | brace-depth + regex header detection | message, service, rpc, enum |
| Everything else | 60-line sliding window, 10-line overlap | windowed chunks |

Each chunk carries: path, area, language, kind, symbol, parent symbol, line range, content hash, imports, and the lineage of `CLAUDE.md` files that govern it (walked upward from the file to the repo root).

### Embedding adapters

| Provider | Dependency | Output dim | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `local` (default) | none | 768 | Deterministic hashed bag-of-tokens. Fully offline, zero setup. Quality is much weaker than a real model — use only for development. |
| `voyage` | `VOYAGE_API_KEY` env | configurable via `--embed-dim` | `voyage-code-3` by default (set `VOYAGE_MODEL` to override). Code-specialized; best retrieval quality. |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` env | configurable via `--embed-dim` | `text-embedding-3-small` by default (set `OPENAI_EMBED_MODEL` to override). |

> Note: API keys are read from environment by convention for the third-party providers (those packages expect that). Everything else is CLI-only.

## Postgres backend

The `pg` backend writes to a schema with two tables (`commits`, `chunks`) plus the `schema_versions` journal. See [migrations/001_init.sql](./migrations/001_init.sql) for the exact DDL, including the HNSW index on `chunks.embedding`.

# codemanagermcp

Model Context Protocol server that exposes **workflow verbs** for AI-driven feature development. An AI agent uses these five tools to move a feature through a defined state machine — without ever touching raw git commands or deployment scripts directly.

```
start_feature  →  push_changes  →  accept_changes  →  (human security review)
                        ↑_____________________|  (if tests fail: fix + retry)
abandon_changes  (at any point, if the feature is scrapped)
```

Based on the [agent-dev-flow](../../specs/agent-dev-flow.md) spec: verbs are **intents**, not mechanisms. Wrong actions are unrepresentable — the agent can't accidentally push to main, destroy the wrong env, or create PRs with broken tests without knowing about it.

## Build

```bash
cd tools/codemanagermcp
npm install
npm run build
```

Produces `dist/server.js`.

## Configure

Configuration is split across two layered files in the same directory as `server.js` (i.e. `tools/codemanagermcp/`):

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `appsettings.json` | Base / dev settings. Safe to commit (no secrets). |
| `release.json` | Production overlay. Wins on every key it defines. Inject at runtime or add to `.gitignore`. |

At least one file must exist. Only include keys in `release.json` that differ from `appsettings.json`.

```bash
cp tools/codemanagermcp/appsettings.example.json tools/codemanagermcp/appsettings.json
cp tools/codemanagermcp/release.example.json     tools/codemanagermcp/release.json
```

**`appsettings.json`** (dev base — no secrets):

```json
{
  "repositoryPath": "C:/absolute/path/to/your/local/clone",
  "mainBranch": "main",
  "branchPrefix": "feat/",
  "azureDevOps": {
    "organization": "MyOrg",
    "project":      "MyProject",
    "repository":   "MyRepo",
    "apiKeyFile":   "./secrets/ado-token.txt"
  },
  "pipelines": {
    "deployPipelineId": 10,
    "ciPipelineId":     12,
    "deletePipelineId": 11,
    "ciTimeoutMinutes": 15
  }
}
```

**`release.json`** (production overlay — injected at build/execution time):

```json
{
  "azureDevOps": {
    "organization": "MyOrg",
    "project":      "MyProject",
    "repository":   "MyRepo"
  },
  "pipelines": {
    "deployPipelineId": 10,
    "deletePipelineId": 11,
    "ciPipelineId":     12,
    "ciTimeoutMinutes": 20
  }
}
```

### Config fields

| Field | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `repositoryPath` | yes | — | Absolute path to the local git clone. |
| `mainBranch` | no | `"main"` | Branch PRs target and features branch from. |
| `branchPrefix` | no | `"feat/"` | Prepended to the slugified feature name. |
| `azureDevOps.organization` | yes | — | ADO organisation (appears after `dev.azure.com/`). |
| `azureDevOps.project` | yes | — | Team project name. |
| `azureDevOps.repository` | yes | — | Repository name as shown in ADO. |
| `azureDevOps.apiKeyFile` | no | — | Path (relative to config dir) to a plain-text file with a PAT. For local dev. Falls back to `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` env var. |
| `pipelines.deployPipelineId` | yes | — | Pipeline definition ID for ephemeral env deploy. Triggered by `start_feature` + `push_changes`. |
| `pipelines.ciPipelineId` | yes | — | Pipeline definition ID for CI (build + tests). Triggered by `accept_changes`. |
| `pipelines.deletePipelineId` | no | — | Pipeline definition ID for env teardown. Triggered by `abandon_changes` + `accept_changes`. |
| `pipelines.ciTimeoutMinutes` | no | `15` | Max minutes to wait for CI pipeline before timing out. |

### Token resolution (priority order)

1. `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` environment variable — set in shell or injected by Azure Pipelines.
2. `azureDevOps.apiKeyFile` contents — path relative to the config dir, for local dev.

In Azure Pipelines, inject the PAT as a secret pipeline variable named `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` and omit `apiKeyFile`. The server will find it via the env var.

Creates a feature branch from main and deploys an ephemeral environment.

| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | Human name, e.g. `"add user auth"`. Auto-slugified. |

### `push_changes`

Stages, commits, and pushes working-tree changes to the active branch, then redeploys.

| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `message` | string | no | Commit message. Default: `"wip: {feature}"`. |
| `stageAll` | boolean | no | Run `git add -A` first. Default: `true`. |

### `accept_changes`

Ensures the branch is pushed, creates a GitHub PR (if a token is configured), runs the configured build + test commands, and returns detailed output. If tests fail, the tool returns the full output so the agent can fix and retry — **no human input required in the loop**.

| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | string | no | PR title. Default: `"feat: {feature}"`. |
| `description` | string | no | PR body. |

### `abandon_changes`

Tears down the environment, deletes local + remote branch, clears state.

| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `force` | boolean | no | Override safety guard when a PR already exists. Default: `false`. |

### `get_status`

Returns current workflow state: active feature, branch, git working-tree status, last commit, and environment status.

No inputs required.

## State machine

```
(idle) ──start_feature──▶ (feature active)
                                │
                         push_changes (repeatable)
                                │
                         accept_changes ──▶ tests pass ──▶ (PR open, awaiting review)
                                │
                         tests fail ──▶ agent fixes ──▶ push_changes ──▶ accept_changes
                                │
                         abandon_changes ──▶ (idle)
```

State is persisted in `data/state.json` (next to the config file) so the server can be restarted mid-feature without losing context.

## Containment model

- **Credential scope**: the GitHub token in config is scoped to one repo. Cross-repo actions are impossible at the GitHub layer.
- **Verb surface**: tools are intents (`start_feature`, `accept_changes`), not mechanisms (`git push`, `kubectl apply`). Wrong actions are unrepresentable.
- **State machine**: each verb is a valid transition; the agent always knows where it is and what comes next.
- **Escalation**: if the agent is stuck it can call `get_status` to re-read state and reason about the next step.

# codemcp

Model Context Protocol server that exposes the [codeindex](../../tools/codeindex/) repository index to coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, any MCP-compatible client). Stdio transport. Backed by either PostgreSQL/pgvector or a local file directory — same interface, swap with one flag.

## Build

```bash
cd src/codemcp
npm install
npm run build
```

Produces `dist/server.js`.

## Invocation

```
node dist/server.js [global-options] <command>
```

`process.cwd()` is the working directory for resolving the config file and `--file-dir`. There is no environment-variable fallback — every value has exactly one source (CLI flag, config file, or built-in default).

### Global options

| Flag | Default | Source priority | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-c, --config <path>` | `./codemcp.config.json` | CLI | Path to the config file (relative to cwd). |
| `-b, --backend <pg\|file>` | `pg` | CLI | Storage backend. |
| `--branch <name>` | `main` | CLI | Default branch to query when a tool call omits `commit`. |
| `--embed-provider <local\|voyage\|openai>` | `local` | CLI | Must match the provider used at index time. |
| `--embed-dim <n>` | `768` | CLI | Must match the indexed commit's dimensionality. |
| `--pg-dsn <dsn>` | from config / built-in | CLI > config > default | Postgres connection string. Prefer the flag for secret injection. |
| `--expected-migration <name>` | `001_init.sql` | CLI | Refuse startup if the backend's latest applied migration is older. |
| `--repository <name>` or `<name:path>` | (none) | CLI | File backend: **`owner/name` only** → data under `tools/codemcp/data/{name}/` (relative to the codemcp package). **`owner/name:absPath`** → `{path}/.codemcp/data/{name}/`. Repeat the flag, **or** pass several entries in one value separated by **`;`**. **Omit entirely** to auto-register every distinct `repository` id found under the default file index (`tools/codeindex/data` when present, else `tools/codemcp/data`). First registration is the fallback default when git `origin` does not match any registered name. |

The file backend reads indexed JSON from disk: either **`tools/codemcp/data/{repository}/...`** when you pass **`--repository owner/name`** (name only), or **`{clone}/.codemcp/data/{repository}/...`** when you pass **`--repository owner/name:/absolute/clone`**. There is no `--file-dir` flag.

Only `connectionString` lives in the optional `codemcp.config.json` file:

```json
{
  "connectionString": "postgres://codeindex_user:CHANGE_ME@localhost:5432/codeindex"
}
```

### `probe <tool> [argsJson]`

## Tool reference

All tools return text in this format so the assistant can quote without hallucinating:

```
repository: <name>  branch: <branch>  commit: <sha7>
---
[<path>:<startLine>-<endLine>] (<language> <kind>) <symbol>  score=<cosine-distance>
commit: <sha>  area: <area>
governed by: <CLAUDE.md paths>
---
<chunk content>
```

The first line is a **resolution header** showing exactly which slice of the index was queried (repository / branch / commit). When `commit` is omitted, the server uses the only indexed snapshot for that repository **and** configured `--branch` when unambiguous; if more than one commit SHA exists for that pair, the tool refuses until you pass `commit` (see `list_commits`).

### Multi-repository support

A single backend can hold commits from multiple repositories. Every commit row carries a `repository` identifier (e.g. `owner/repo` from the indexer, or a path-based id), set at publish time.

**File backend — multiple `--repository name:path` flags (or one flag with `name:path` pairs separated by `;`), or auto-discovery:**

- With **explicit** registrations, each gets its own on-disk reader; **all are searchable** by passing the tool argument `repository` equal to that registration's **`name`** (the part before the first `:` in each pair).
- With **no** `--repository` flags and a migrated file index (`schema_versions.json` under the default data dir), the server **scans published commits** and registers every distinct `repository` field (same as listing each name with `--repository`). All share one physical tree when using sibling `tools/codeindex/data`.
- **`search_code`**, **`find_symbol`**, and **`get_file_context`** query **one** repo per call. If you omit `repository`, they use **git `origin`** when it matches a registered name, else the **first** registration (explicit order or sorted discovery order).
- **`list_commits`** with no `repository` filter **aggregates** every registered repo (sorted by `indexed_at`); pass `repository` to narrow to one name.

**Postgres backend:** one connection; multiple logical repos live in the same DB and are distinguished by the `repository` column. Pass `repository` on tool calls to target the right rows.

**When no `--repository` flags are passed (file backend):**

- If `schema_versions.json` exists under the default file index directory, **every distinct `repository` id** in published `commit.json` files is registered automatically (see above).
- Otherwise (legacy single-tree layout): the server **auto-detects** a default from `git config --get remote.origin.url` in `process.cwd()` when possible. If detection fails, tools that need a repo may refuse until you pass `repository` explicitly.

**Postgres / file with no migrated index:** same as before — git-origin default when possible.

### `search_code`

Semantic vector search. Best when you don't know the exact symbol name and want code by intent.

**Input**

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `query` | string | yes | Natural-language or code-fragment query. |
| `k` | integer 1–50 | no (default 8) | Number of results. |
| `area` | enum | no | `api`, `backend`, `frontend`, `db`, `test`, `docs`, `tools`, `pipeline`, `minikube`, `root`. |
| `kind` | enum | no | `class`, `method`, `function`, `component`, `interface`, `record`, `section`, `statement`, `message`, `service`, `rpc`, `file`, `window`. |
| `language` | string | no | `csharp`, `typescript`, `tsx`, `javascript`, `jsx`, `markdown`, `sql`, `protobuf`, `json`. |
| `repository` | string | no | Repo id to query (must match a `--repository` **name** when several are registered). Defaults to the first registration or auto-detected repo. |
| `commit` | string | no | Full SHA. **Required** when more than one distinct SHA is indexed for the same `repository` + `--branch`; otherwise defaults to the sole snapshot. Use `list_commits` to list SHAs. |

**Probe example**

```bash

# bash / zsh / git-bash
probe search_code '{"query":"migration runner with checksum","k":3,"area":"tools"}'
```

```powershell

# PowerShell
probe search_code '{\"query\":\"migration runner with checksum\",\"k\":3,\"area\":\"tools\"}'
```

### `get_file_context`

Returns every chunk for a given file, plus the governing `CLAUDE.md` files. Use before editing a file the assistant hasn't seen.

**Input**

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | Repository-relative path, forward slashes. |
| `repository` | string | no | Repo id; match a `--repository` **name** when several are registered. Defaults to first registration or auto-detected repo. |
| `commit` | string | no | Full SHA. **Required** when more than one distinct SHA is indexed for the same `repository` + `--branch`; otherwise defaults to the sole snapshot. Use `list_commits` to list SHAs. |

**Probe example**

```bash

# bash / zsh / git-bash

```

```powershell

```

### `list_commits`

Enumerate indexed commit snapshots.

**Input**

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `branch` | string | no | Restrict to a single branch. |
| `repository` | string | no | Restrict to a single repository. (Unlike the search tools, `list_commits` does NOT default to the current repo — it lists everything by default.) |
| `limit` | integer 1–100 | no (default 10) | Max rows. |

**Probe example**

```bash

# bash / zsh / git-bash
probe list_commits '{"branch":"main","limit":5}'
```

```powershell

# PowerShell
probe list_commits '{\"branch\":\"main\",\"limit\":5}'
```

Configure **`codemcp` in `~/.cursor/mcp.json`** (user MCP). Example:

- **`args`**: start with the **absolute** path to `tools/codemcp/dist/server.js` (Cursor sometimes runs MCP with `cwd` under your home directory, so a repo-relative path resolves to `/Users/you/tools/...` and fails).

See [mcp.json.example](./mcp.json.example). Run `npm install && npm run build` under `tools/codemcp` after upgrades, ensure **`tools/codeindex/data/`** exists with migrations + commits (see below), then reload MCP.

With **`--repository Platform/Rxo.Platform.Web.Sandbox`** (no `:path`), codemcp **prefers** the sibling indexer output **`tools/codeindex/data/`** when `schema_versions.json` exists there (normal layout after `npm run migrate:file` / `publish:file` in `tools/codeindex`). No copy into `tools/codemcp/data/...` is required in that setup.

If you keep index files only under `tools/codemcp/data/<owner>/<repo>/` instead, ensure that tree includes `schema_versions.json` (and `commits/<sha>/...`) — codemcp does **not** create that directory for you.
